work.title: Oratio 14: De pauperum amore

paragraphs.text:
…all of you, in need of divine grace as well, even if one seems to surpass another, for each is measured by small measures: receive this discourse on love for the poor, not meagerly but generously, so that you may become rich in the kingdom. And pray that I may supply it to you richly, feed your souls with the word, and break the spiritual bread for the hungry. I might rain down food from heaven, like Moses of old, and bestow the bread of angels. Or I might feed thousands and tens of thousands with a few loaves in the desert, as Jesus did later, he who is the true bread and the source of true life. It is not at all easy to find which virtue prevails over the rest and give it first rank and the prize of victory. In the same way, in a fragrant meadow full of flowers it is not easy to find the most beautiful and most fragrant one, since first one flower and then another draws our sight and smell to itself and persuades us to pick it first. In my opinion, then, we should consider and distinguish these things as follows.

2. Faith, hope and love, these three, are good. The witness to faith is Abraham, who was justified by faith. The witness to hope is Enosh, who first hoped to call upon the Lord, along with all the righteous who suffered hardship for the sake of hope. The witness to love is the divine Apostle, who dared to say something even against himself for Israel's sake, and God himself, who is called love. Hospitality is good. Its witness among the righteous is Lot the Sodomite, though he was no Sodomite in his ways; among sinners it is Rahab the harlot, though she was no harlot in her intention, for she was praised and saved because of her hospitality. Brotherly love is good, and its witness is Jesus, who consented not only to be called our brother but also to suffer for us. Love for humankind is good, and its witness is the same Jesus. He not only made man for good works and joined the image to the dust, to guide him to the noblest things and win him the things above, but also became man for our sake. Long-suffering is good, and the same Jesus is its witness. He not only refused the legions of angels against those who rose up and acted as tyrants against him, and not only rebuked Peter for raising the sword, but also restored the ear of the man who had been struck. Stephen, the disciple of Christ, later did the same, [?]

praying for those who were stoning him. Meekness is good, and its witnesses are Moses and David, who were attested for it above all others, and their teacher too, who did not quarrel or cry out or raise his voice in the streets, and did not resist those who led him away.

3. Zeal is good, and Phinehas bears witness to it. He ran the Midianite woman through together with the Israelite, to take away the reproach from the sons of Israel, and became renowned for his choice. After him come those who say, "I have been very zealous for the Lord," and "I am jealous for you with a godly jealousy," and "Zeal for your house will consume me." They did not only say this but also suffered for it. Disciplining the body is good. Let Paul persuade you of this, who was still disciplining himself and who used the example of Israel to frighten those who trust in themselves and indulge the body. Let Jesus himself persuade you too, who fasted, was tempted and conquered the tempter. Prayer and vigil are good. Let God persuade you of this, who kept vigil and prayed before his passion. Purity and virginity are good. Let Paul persuade you of this, who made laws about these things and judged fairly between marriage and celibacy. Let Jesus himself persuade you too, who was born of a Virgin so as both to honor birth and to honor virginity above it. Self-control is good. Let David persuade you of this. When he gained the well in Bethlehem he did not drink from it but only poured out the water as an offering, refusing to satisfy his own desire at the cost of another's [?]

4. Solitude and quiet are good. Elijah's Carmel teaches me this, and John's desert, and Jesus' mountain, to which he is often seen withdrawing to be alone in quiet. Frugality is good. Elijah teaches me this, lodging with a widow, and John, clothed in camel's hair, and Peter, living on a penny's worth of lupines. Humility is good, and its examples are many and come from many quarters. First among them is the Savior and Master of all. He not only humbled himself to the form of a servant, and not only gave his face to the shame of spitting and was counted among the lawless, he who [?] [Note: (29) Μαδιανῖτιν: Or. 2 reads Μαδιανίτην.]

…[washing] the feet of his disciples in the guise of a slave. Poverty and contempt for money are good, and Zacchaeus bears witness to it, and Christ himself. At Christ's coming into his house, Zacchaeus gave almost everything away as fruit; Christ, for his part, made this the mark of perfection for the rich man. To speak of these things more briefly still: contemplation is good, and action is good. Contemplation rises up from here, advances into the Holy of Holies and leads our mind back to what is akin to it. Action receives Christ, serves him and proves love by deeds. [?]

5. We must open our hearts to all the poor and to all who suffer for any reason whatever, according to the commandment that bids us rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. Being human ourselves, we must be the first to bring to our fellow humans our contribution of kindness, whether they need it because they are widowed or orphaned, or exiled from their homeland, or because of cruel masters, or insolent rulers, or [?] [Notes: some read ἐπανιστῶσα, and rightly. [?] (38) Ed. ἀπανιστᾶσα. [?] Or. 2 reads προπορεύεται. (39) Ἐπανάγουσα: "lifting up, raising." [?] (40) Τοῖς ἔργοις: [?] τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἔρ[γοις], "by good works."]

…the inhumanity of tax collectors, or the bloodthirstiness of robbers, or the greed of thieves, or confiscation, or shipwreck. All of them are equally to be pitied. They look to our hands just as we look to God's for whatever we need. And among them, those who suffer undeservedly are more pitiable than those used to misfortune. Most of all, we must open our hearts to those destroyed by the sacred disease. They are eaten away down to the flesh, the bones and the marrow, as is threatened against some, and are betrayed by this wretched, lowly and faithless body. How I came to be joined to it I do not know, nor how I am both the image of God and mixed with clay. When it is healthy it makes war on me, and when it is attacked it grieves me. I love it as a fellow servant and turn from it as an enemy. I flee it as a chain and respect it as a fellow heir. I strive to wear it down, yet I have no other helper to use for the noblest things, since I know what I was made for and that I must ascend to God through my actions.

7. I spare it as a fellow worker, yet I do not know how to escape its revolt, or how to avoid falling away from God, weighed down by fetters that drag me down or hold me to the ground. It is a kindly enemy and a treacherous friend. What a union, and what an estrangement! What I fear, I cherish, and what I love, I dread. Before I go to war with it I am reconciled, and before I make peace I fall out with it. What is this wisdom concerning me? What is this great mystery? Perhaps God wishes this: we are a portion of God and have flowed down from above, and so might grow proud and puffed up because of our dignity and despise our Creator. To prevent this, he wants us to keep looking to him in our struggle with the body, and wants the weakness joined to us to be a schooling for our dignity. Then we may know that we are at once the greatest and the lowliest, earthly and heavenly, temporal and immortal, heirs of light or of fire, that is, of darkness, depending on which way we incline. Such is our compound nature, and the reason for it, so it seems to me, is this: when we are lifted up because of the image, we are humbled because of the dust. Let whoever wishes philosophize about these things; we too will philosophize with him at a more suitable time.

8. But now, as my discourse set out to say, grieving as I do for my own flesh and for my own weakness in the sufferings of others: we must care, brothers, for what is akin to us and our fellow servant. For even if I accused it as an enemy because of its passions, I still embrace it as a friend because of the one who bound us together. We must care for our neighbors' bodies no less than each of us cares for his own, both the healthy and those consumed by this same disease. For we are all one in the Lord, whether rich or poor, slave or free, healthy or sick in body. There is one head of all, Christ, from whom all things come, and what the members are to one another, each of us is to each, and all to all. So we must not overlook or neglect those who have fallen before us into our common weakness. We should not rejoice that our own bodies are well so much as mourn that our brothers' bodies are in a wretched state. We should consider that the one security for our own flesh and souls is kindness toward them. Let us look at it this way.

9. For others there is only one thing to pity, their poverty, and perhaps time, or work, or a friend or relative, or a change of circumstances may relieve it. For these people poverty is no less a burden, and perhaps even more, since they cannot work and help themselves. Along with their flesh they have been robbed of the necessities of life, and their fear of the disease is always greater than their hope of health. So they get very little help from hope, which is the only medicine for the unfortunate. On top of poverty, the disease is a second evil, the most dreaded and heaviest of evils, and the one most readily on many people's lips as a curse. Third, people will not come near them or even look at them; they are shunned and loathed and avoided as though accursed. This is heavier for them than the disease itself, when they realize that they are hated for their misfortune. For my part, I cannot bear their suffering without tears, and I am shaken just remembering it. May you feel the same, so that by tears you may escape tears. And I know that all those present who love Christ and love the poor, who have mercy as God's own and from God, do feel it. You yourselves are witnesses of their suffering. [Notes: (62) Some read: "For even if I accused it as an enemy because of its passions." (64) Ἢ ἕκαστον: Or. 2 and Reg. c read ἢ ἑκάστῳ. (66) Εὖ ἡμῖν ἔχει: most codices read ἡμῖν εὖ [?]]

…"You will live with wild beasts, a rock will be your shelter, and of all people only the most devout will see you." And she adds those pitiful words of Job: "Why were you formed in your mother's womb? Why did you come out of the womb and not perish at once, so that death ran together with birth? Why did you not depart before your time, before tasting the evils of life? Why did knees receive you? Why did you suck at the breast, when you were to live wretchedly, a life harsher than death?" She says this and pours out fountains of tears. The unhappy woman longs to embrace her child, but she fears his flesh as an enemy. Outcries and persecutions arise from the whole people, not against wrongdoers but against the unfortunate. A man has been known to live with a murderer, and to share not only his roof but his table with an adulterer, to choose a temple robber as the companion of his life, and to make peace with those who did him harm. Yet he turned away from one who had done him no injury at all, as though his suffering were a crime. Wickedness fares better than disease: we embrace inhumanity as if it were nobility and despise compassion as if it were shameful.

12. They are driven from cities, driven from houses, from the marketplace, from gatherings, from roads, from festivals, from banquets, and even (what suffering!) from water itself. Not even flowing springs are shared between them and other people… [Notes: (90) Πέτρα: Reg. c reads πέτραι. (93) Εὐθύς: some read εὐθέως. (94) Τί δέ σοι συνήντησε, etc.: Reg. c reads συνήν[τησαν] [?]. (95) Ἀθλίως: Reg. c adds οὕτως. (96) Περιπτύξασθαι: Or. 2 reads περιπτύξεσθαι. (98) Διατεθεικόσι [?]. (99) Ἀπεστράφη: some read [?].]

…[not the one] who met their need, but the one who did not send them away harshly. Most of them do not even avoid the festivals out of shame. On the contrary, need drives them to push their way into them. I mean these public and sacred festivals which we have devised for the healing of souls, when we gather for some mystery or celebrate the martyrs of the truth, so that we may imitate the piety of those whose contests we honor. Being human, they are ashamed before people because of their misfortune, and would rather be hidden by mountains, or cliffs, or forests, or at last by night and darkness. Yet they throw themselves into our midst, a pitiable cargo that deserves our tears. Perhaps there is a reason for this: that they may remind us of our own weakness and persuade us not to cling to anything present and visible as though it were lasting. They throw themselves forward, some longing for a human voice, others for the sight of a face, others to gather a little provision for life from those who live in luxury, and all of them hoping to find some gentleness by making their laments public.

13. Who is not broken by their wailing as they join together in a piteous chorus? What ear can bear the sound, what eye can endure the sight? Some lie beside one another, wretchedly yoked together by the disease, each contributing some feature of the misfortune to the common store of pity. They add to one another's suffering: pitiable for their illness, and more pitiable for sharing it. Around them stands a mixed crowd of onlookers who sympathize, but only for a moment. Others roll at people's feet in the sun and dust. Sometimes they are tormented by bitter frosts, rainstorms and raging winds, and they escape being trampled only because we loathe even to touch them. The wailing of their pleas sounds against the sacred chants inside, and a piteous lament rises up against the mystic voices. Why must I set out their whole misfortune before people celebrating a feast? Perhaps I could move even you to lament if I told it all in detail like a tragedy, and their suffering would overcome the festival. I say these things because I cannot yet persuade you that grief is sometimes more precious than pleasure, and sorrow than festivity, and that a tear can be more praiseworthy than laughter that is not fitting.

14. Such is their condition, and it is far more wretched than I have described. Yet they are our brothers before God, even if you do not wish it. They have been given the same nature as we have and were fashioned from the same clay from which we were first made. They are strung together with sinews and bones just as we are, and clothed in skin and flesh like everyone else, as the divine Job says somewhere when he philosophizes about his sufferings and scorns our outward appearance. Or rather, to say the greater thing, they received the image just as we did, and perhaps keep it better than we do, even though their bodies have decayed. They have put on the same Christ in the inner man and have been entrusted with the same pledge of the Spirit. They share with us the same laws, oracles, covenants, assemblies, mysteries and hopes. Christ, who takes away the sin of the whole world, died for them just as for us. They are fellow heirs of the life above, even if they have largely missed out on the life here. They are buried with Christ and rise with him, if indeed they suffer with him so that they may also be glorified with him.

15. And what of us? We have inherited the great and new name of being called after Christ. We are the holy nation, the royal priesthood, the special and chosen people, zealous for good and saving works. We are disciples of Christ, the meek and loving one, who bore our weaknesses, who humbled himself even to our own lump of clay, who for our sake became poor in this flesh and earthly tent, and suffered and was afflicted for us, so that we might be enriched with divinity. What then shall we do, who have received so great an example of compassion and sympathy? What shall we think about these people, and what shall we do? Shall we overlook them? Pass them by? Abandon them as dead, as abominable, as the worst of reptiles and beasts? By no means, brothers! This does not befit us, the flock of Christ the good Shepherd, who brings back the straying, seeks the lost and strengthens the weak. Nor does it befit human nature, which has made compassion its law, learning piety and kindness from our common weakness. [Notes: [?] (21) Παραπολύ: some read παρὰ πολύ. (25) Ἵνα ἡμεῖς: Regg. [?] read ἵν' ἡμεῖς. (26) Τὴν θεότητα: Reg. c and others read τὴν ἐκείνου θεότητα, "his divinity"; in [?] τήν is missing.]

…while we live in splendid houses decorated with all kinds of stones, gleaming with gold and silver, with fine mosaic work and colorful paintings, lures to deceive the eye? Some houses we shall live in, others we shall build. For whom? Perhaps not even for our heirs but for strangers and outsiders, and perhaps not even for those who love us but for those who hate and envy us most, which is the worst of evils. They will shiver in worn and tattered rags, or perhaps will not even have those. Meanwhile we shall pamper ourselves with soft, flowing clothes and airy fabrics of linen and silk. Some of these will make us look indecent rather than handsome (that is what I call everything superfluous and overelaborate), while the rest will be stored away inside, a useless and unprofitable worry, food for moths and for time, which consumes all things. They will not even have the food they need (O my luxury and their misery!), but will lie before our doors, fainting and starving. Their bodies do not even give them the means to beg. They have no voice to lament with, no hands to stretch out in supplication, no feet to approach those who have plenty, no breath to give strength to their dirge. They count the heaviest of evils the lightest, and are grateful for their eyes only because they cannot see their own mutilation.

17. That is their condition. Meanwhile we recline, splendid and in splendor, on high and lofty couches spread with superfluous coverings too fine to touch, and we are annoyed if we so much as hear the voice of their pleas. Our floor must be fragrant with flowers, often out of season, and our table sprinkled with perfumes, the most fragrant and costly kind, so that we may grow even softer. Servants must stand by, some in finery, their hair carefully arranged over their faces, adorned more than [?] [Notes: [?] (54) Ἀνακεισόμεθα: Par. reads ἀναβησόμεθα, "we shall go up." (55) Τῶν αἰτήσεων: missing in Par.]

…is good for lustful eyes; others holding the cups on their fingertips as gracefully and securely as they can; others contriving a breeze over our heads with fans, cooling the bulk of our flesh with breezes made by hand. On top of all this, the table must be loaded with meats, all the elements of air, earth and water supplying us richly, and crowded with the trickery of cooks and confectioners. Everyone must compete to see who can best flatter our greedy and ungrateful belly, that heavy burden and source of evils, that most insatiable and faithless beast, which will soon be destroyed along with the foods that are destroyed. For them it is a great thing to have their fill even of water, while for us the bowls of wine run to drunkenness, or rather beyond drunkenness for the more dissolute. One wine we send back, another we approve for its bouquet, about yet another we philosophize, and we think it a loss if beside the local wine there is not also one of the so-called foreign wines, ruling like a tyrant. For we must be, or be thought to be, lavish and beyond our needs, as though we were ashamed not to be thought wicked and slaves of the belly and of what lies below the belly.

18. Why do we do this, friends and brothers? Why are we also sick in our souls, with a sickness far worse than that of the body? The one is involuntary, while the other comes from choice. The one ends with this life, while the other goes with us when we depart. The one is pitied, while the other is hated, at least by those who have sense. Why do we not come to nature's aid while we have the opportunity? Why do we, who are flesh, not cover the humiliation of the flesh? Why do we live in luxury amid our brothers' misfortunes? May I never be rich while they are in want, nor healthy unless I help heal their wounds. May I never have enough food or clothing, or rest under a roof, unless I also offer them bread, share my clothing as far as I can, and give them rest under a roof. But either we must give up everything to Christ, [Note: (58) Λίχνην: several Regii read λίχνον.]

…may be sanctified through being in a good state, and through sharing with those who have nothing. But if I should sow for myself alone, then may I sow and others eat; and, to quote Job again, instead of wheat may nettles come up for me, and instead of barley a bramble; may a scorching wind catch up and a whirlwind carry off my labours, so that I may have toiled in vain. And if I should build barns, storing up the treasures of mammon, and [?] of mammon, may my soul be required of me this very night, and may I have to give account of what I wickedly stored up.

19. Shall we not come to our senses, at long last? Shall we not cast off our callousness, not to call it our stinginess? Shall we not take account of the human condition? Shall we not set our own affairs right through the misfortunes of others? For by nature nothing human is stable, nor even, nor self-sufficient, nor does it remain in the same state; rather, a kind of wheel runs round our affairs, bringing now one change, now another, often within a single day, and sometimes even within an hour. One could sooner trust the breezes, which never stand still, or the wake of a ship crossing the sea, or the deceptive dreams of the night, whose charm lasts only a little while, or the figures that children shape in the sand at play, than human prosperity. Wise, then, are those who, because they do not trust the present, store up the future for themselves; and who, because human good fortune is unstable and uneven, love the kindness that never falls, so that they may gain at least one of three things in any case: either never to fare badly, since God often rewards the pious with good things even here, kindness calling forth compassion; or to have confidence within themselves toward God, as people who have suffered not because of wickedness but because of some dispensation; or, lastly, to claim as a debt from those who are prospering the kindness which they themselves showed beforehand to those in need, when they were faring well.

20. "Let not the wise man boast," it says, "in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his wealth, nor the strong man in his strength," even if they have reached the very summit, the one of wisdom, the other of riches, the other of power. But I will add what follows from these: nor let the illustrious man boast in his glory, nor the robust man in his health, nor the handsome man in his bloom, nor the young man in his youth, nor, to put it briefly, in anything else of the things praised here, the man who is puffed up by it; but let him who boasts boast in this… Job 31:40. (48) Φάγοιεν: two Regii and Or. 2 read φάγοισαν.

…a serpent by the way, neither lying in wait for the heel nor having his head lain in wait for. But to the rest of us the same David rightly cries out, like some herald with the loudest of voices from a lofty platform proclaiming to all the people, calling us heavy of heart and lovers of falsehood: not to cling too closely to the things we see, nor to suppose that all happiness here consists in nothing other than a surfeit of grain and wine, things that perish. And perhaps the blessed Micah too had this in mind when, rising up against the things that go along the ground and only seem good, he says: "Draw near to the everlasting mountains; arise and go, for this is not your rest." This is almost in harmony, even in its very words, with what our Lord and Saviour commands. Saying what? "Rise, let us go hence"—not only removing the disciples of that time from that one place, as one might think, but always drawing all his disciples from earth and earthly things to the heavens and heavenly things.

22. So then, let us now follow the Word; let us seek the rest that is there; let us throw away the abundance that is here. Whatever is good in it, let us gain that alone: let us acquire our souls by almsgiving, let us share what we have with the poor, so that we may be rich in the things that are there. Give a portion to the soul too, not only to the flesh; give a portion to God too, not only to the world. Take something away from the belly and consecrate it to the Spirit; snatch something from the fire and set it far from the flame that feeds here below; snatch it from the tyrant and entrust it to the Master. Give a portion to seven, that is, to this life, and also to eight, to the life that will receive us after this one. Give a little to him from whom you have the greater part; give even the whole to him who has bestowed all things on you. You will never outdo the munificence of God, even if you give away all that you have, even if you add yourself to what you have. For this too is receiving: to be given to God. However much you contribute, what remains is always more; and you will give nothing of your own, for all things come from God. And just as one cannot overstep one's own shadow, which retreats as far as we advance and always keeps the same distance ahead, nor can the body's height rise above the head, which always lies

above the body, so neither can we outdo God in what we give. For we give nothing outside what is his, nor beyond his generosity.

23. Recognise where you got your existence, your breath, your understanding, and, the greatest thing of all, your knowing God, your hope of the kingdom of heaven, equal honour with the angels, the vision of glory—now in mirrors and riddles, but then more perfect and more pure—your becoming a son of God, a co-heir with Christ, and, I dare to say, a god yourself. Where did all these things come to you from, and from whom? Or, to speak of small and visible things, who gave you to behold the beauty of the sky, the course of the sun, the circle of the moon, the multitude of the stars, and the harmony and order that holds in all of them alike, as in a lyre; the changes of the hours, the alternations of the seasons, the cycles of the years, the equal sharing of day and night, the produce of the earth, the outpouring of the air, the breadth of the sea, both unbound and held in place, the depths of rivers, the currents of the winds? Who gave you rains, farming, food, arts, dwellings, laws, commonwealths, a civilised life, friendship with your own kind? How is it that some animals have been tamed and yoked for you, while others have been given to you as food? Who appointed you lord and king of all things on earth? Who, not to go through them one by one, bestowed on you everything by which man excels the other creatures? Is it not he who now, before all things and in place of all things, asks kindness of you? Then are we not ashamed if, having received so much from him and hoping for still more, we will not bring God even this one thing, kindness? He separated us from the beasts and honoured us alone of all creatures on earth with reason; and shall we turn ourselves into beasts? Have we been so corrupted by luxury, or gone so mad, or—I do not know what to call it—that because of our bread and bran, which we have perhaps acquired wrongly, we shall think ourselves better than they are even by nature? And just as there was once, as far as the myths go, a race of giants set apart from the rest of men, shall we too be lofty and superhuman compared with these, like that famous Nimrod, or the race of Anak who once oppressed Israel, or those on whose account the flood cleansed the earth? He is not ashamed to be called our Father, though he is God and Master; and shall we deny even our kinship? (85) Σελήνης: Reg. a, ἢ σελήνης. (85) Σελήνης: Reg. a, ἢ σελήνης. (88) Πάντων κατέστησε: so Regg. a, c, d, bm, ph, etc. In the editions, κατέστησε πάντων. (89) Φιλάνθρωπον: Reg. a, φιλάδελφον. [?] (90) Ἐχώρισε: Reg. bm and Or. 2, ἐχώρησε [?]

24. By no means, friends and brethren, let us become bad stewards of what has been given to us, lest we hear Peter saying: "Be ashamed, you who hold on to what belongs to others; imitate the equity of God, and no one will be poor." Let us not toil at hoarding and guarding while others toil in poverty, lest we be reproached and bitterly threatened, on the one hand by the divine Amos in these words: "Come now, you who say, When will the new moon be over, so that we may sell, and the Sabbaths, so that we may open our storehouses?"—and the words that follow, in which he holds out the wrath of God over those who keep a large and a small measure; and on the other hand by the blessed Micah. Perhaps he is striking at luxury itself, since satiety gives birth to insolence: lolling on ivory couches, pampering oneself with the finest of ointments, fattening on tender calves from the herds and kids from the flocks, clapping along to the sound of instruments, and, still more, supposing that any of these things is stable and lasting. But perhaps he considered these things less terrible than the fact that, living in luxury, they felt nothing for the affliction of Joseph; for this is what he adds to the charge of surfeit. Let us not suffer this now, nor indulge ourselves so much that we also despise the kindness of God, who is displeased at these things, even if he does not bring his wrath upon sinners hard on the heels of their wickedness.

25. Let us imitate God's highest and first law, who sends rain on the righteous and on sinners and makes the sun rise on all alike. He spread out the earth free for all creatures of the land, and springs, and rivers, and forests; the air for winged creatures, and the water for all whose life is in the water. He bestowed the first means of living abundantly on all, not held under anyone's power, not limited by law, not divided by boundaries, but set them forth common and rich, and in no way poorer on that account. So he honoured the equal dignity of nature by the equality of his gift, and showed the wealth of his own goodness. But men, having buried away gold and silver, and clothing that is soft and beyond what is needed, and translucent stones, and anything else of the kind—things that are the marks of war, and of faction, and of the first tyranny—then raise (1) Ἐμπωλήσωμεν… ἀνοίξωμεν: Regg. and Or. 2, ἐμπωλήσομεν… ἀνοίξομεν. (6) [?] in the editions, τοιοῦτο… στάσεων. In some, τοσοῦ[?]. (7) Γνωρίσματα: Or. 2, γνώρισμα.

their brows in their folly and shut out mercy from the unfortunate among their kin, unwilling to help others in their necessities even out of their superfluities—what ignorance! what boorishness!—not considering, if nothing else, at least this: that poverty and wealth, and what we call freedom and slavery, and names of that kind, entered the human race later, like common diseases that broke in together with wickedness and are its inventions. "But from the beginning," it says, "it was not so." Rather, he who fashioned man in the beginning left him free and self-determining, ruled only by the law of the commandment, and rich in the delights of paradise; and this he both willed for the rest of the human race and bestowed on it through the one first seed. Freedom and wealth consisted solely in keeping the commandment; true poverty and slavery, in transgressing it.

26. But once envy and quarrels came in, and the deceitful tyranny of the serpent, which keeps luring us on with the bait of pleasure and stirs up the bolder against the weaker, kinship was torn apart into the estrangement of names, and greed cut up the nobility of nature, taking law as well to be the ally of domination. But you, I beg you, look to the original equality, not to the later division; not to the law of the one who has gained the upper hand, but to the law of the Creator. Help nature as far as you are able; honour the ancient freedom; respect yourself; cover the disgrace of your race; come to the aid of disease; [relieve] want

…has of God; even if the one does greater good and the other less, each, I think, according to his own power. He made man, and after dissolving him gathers him together again; but you, do not overlook one who has fallen. He showed mercy in the greatest things: he gave the law besides everything else, and the prophets, and before these the natural law, the unwritten [?] examiner of our actions; he reproved, admonished, educated; and finally he gave himself as a ransom for the life of the world, bestowing apostles, evangelists, teachers, shepherds, healings, wonders, a return to life, the destruction of death, a trophy over the one who had conquered, a covenant in shadow, a covenant in truth, the distributions of the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the new salvation. And you, if you are able to do the greater things too, those by which a soul is benefited (for God has made you rich in these as well, if you are willing), do not hold back from doing good to the needy in these either. Rather, first and foremost give to him who asks you, and even before you are asked, all day long showing mercy and lending the word, and diligently demanding back the loan with interest—the progress of the one you have helped, which always adds to the word—so increasing in yourself little by little the seeds of piety. But if not, then at least help with the second and lesser things, as far as lies within your power: offer food, offer a rag, bring medicine, bind up wounds, ask something about his misfortune, speak wisely about endurance, take heart, go near. You will surely not be any the worse for it; you will surely not catch the disease, even if the overly delicate think so, deceived by idle talk—or rather they put this forward as a defence of their own caution, or their impiety, taking refuge in cowardice as though it were something great and wise. Let these persuade you: reason, and the physicians, and those who live with these people and nurse them, none of whom has yet come into danger by going near them. You, then, even if the thing is fearful and gives grounds for suspicion, servant of Christ, lover of God and lover of mankind, do not give way to anything ignoble. Take courage in faith; let compassion conquer cowardice, and the fear of God conquer squeamishness; let piety stand before carnal reasonings. Do not overlook, do not pass by your brother; do not turn away from him as from a curse, a pollution, or anything else to be shunned and forbidden. He is your own limb, even if misfortune has [?] (24) Συνάγει: Jes., συνεισάγει. (25) Παρίδῃς: Reg. bm, παρείδῃς. (28) Δανείζων: Or. 1 and 2, δανίζων. (29) Ὠφελημένου: Reg. bm, ὠφελουμένου. νουνεχῶς αὔξων ἐν ἑαυτῷ, "who prudently in himself"

[?]. "To you the poor man has been left," as to God, even if you pass him by too haughtily—for perhaps I shall shame you with these words. Here lies before you an occasion for kindness, even if the stranger estranges you from receiving good [?].

28. Everyone who sails is near shipwreck, and the more so the more boldly he sails; and everyone who is clothed in a body is near the evils of the body, and the more so the more upright he walks and fails to see those lying before him. While you sail with a fair wind, give a hand to the one who is shipwrecked; while you are healthy and rich, help the one who is suffering. Do not wait to learn in your own person how great an evil inhumanity is, and how great a good it is to open one's heart to the needy. Do not wish God to raise his hand against those who hold their necks high and pass by the poor. Learn these things from the misfortunes of others. Give something, however little, to the needy; for it is not little to one who lacks everything, nor to God, if it is according to your means. Give eagerness in place of a great gift. If you have nothing, weep. A great medicine for the unfortunate is mercy offered from the soul, and genuinely sharing in their pain relieves much of the misfortune. Man is not of less worth to you, O man, than the beast, which the law commands you to lift up if it has fallen into a pit, or to bring back if it has strayed. Whether the law hides something else in this, more secret and deeper, as is the case with much of the depth and double sense of the law, it is not for me to know, but for the Spirit, who searches and knows all things. But what I do grasp, as far as my reason reaches, is that it trains us through kindness in small things toward a kindness that is more perfect and greater. For how much kindness is owed to those of the same race and the same dignity, if it is required even toward irrational animals?

29. This, then, is what reason says, and the law, and the most reasonable of men, among whom doing good is more prized than receiving it, and mercy more eagerly sought than gain. And what would you say of our own wise men? For I pass over those outside, who find gods to be the advocates of their passions, and to the god of gain, to whom (57) Ἐγκαταλέλειπται: Reg. bm, ἐγκαταλείπεται. [?]

…they assign the first place. And already, what is worse than this, there are some who regard even the murder of human beings as [part of the worship] of demons, and among certain nations inhumanity is actually part of piety; they themselves delight in such sacrifices, and suppose their gods do too, becoming wicked priests and initiates of wicked beings. But there are some of our own—a thing worth weeping over—who are so far from sharing the pain of those who suffer and helping them that they even bitterly reproach them and trample on them. They philosophise empty and vain things; they truly speak from the earth and talk into the air, and not into understanding ears accustomed to divine doctrines; and they dare to say: "Their misery comes from God, and our prosperity comes from God. And who am I to undo a decree of God and to show myself kinder than God? Let them suffer, let them be miserable, let them be unfortunate: so it has been decided." Only here are they lovers of God, where they must guard their obols and swagger against the wretched. That they do not in fact believe their prosperity comes from God, they show clearly by what they say. For who, knowing God as the giver of what he possesses, would think in this way about those in need? For it belongs to the same people both to have something from God and to use what they have according to God.

30. And whether their suffering comes from God is not yet clear, so long as matter of its own accord carries disorder, as in a current. And who knows whether one man is being punished for wickedness while another is exalted as worthy of praise—and not the reverse, that one is exalted because of wickedness while another is tested because of virtue? The one is lifted up higher so that he may fall more heavily, being allowed first to let his whole wickedness break out, like a disease, so that he may also be punished more justly; the other is pressed down even beyond expectation, so that, tested like gold in the furnace, he may melt away whatever wickedness he has, even if it is small. For no one is wholly clean of filth, not in a nature that is born, as we have heard, even if he seems more approved. We find some such mystery in divine Scripture too, and it would take long to list all the sayings of the Spirit that lead me to this. But who could measure the sand of the seas, and the drops of rain, and the length of the deep? And who could trace out the depth of God's wisdom concerning all things, by which [?] (63) Χορηγόν: [?] χορηγόν. (57) Προσεπεμβαίνουσι: [?] bm, ph and Or. 2, Pan., προσεπεμβαίνοντες. The editions, ἐπεμβαίνουσι. (65) Πλεῖον, etc.: three Regii, πλέον. In [?] it reads: πλεῖον ἐπαιρόμενος, ὥσπερ τινὰ νόσον [?] ἑαυτοῦ κακίαν συγχωρηθείς, ἵνα πέσῃ χαλεπώτερον [?]. (58) [?] συνηθισμένας. (59) Ταλαιπωρείτωσαν: Or. 2, ταλαιπωρήτω[?]σαν [?]. (60) [?] on the authority of several [?]; in Latin, οὐ γοῦν [?] Regg. 1 and 2, Or. 2, Pan., etc. (68) Τοιοῦτο: Regg. bm and ph, τοιοῦτον. (69) [?] ph. The editions, αὐ- [?]. (70) Καί: Reg. d, ἤ.

…he both made all things and governs them in the way that he himself wills and [?]? For it is enough, following the divine Apostle, simply to marvel at how hard it is to discern and to behold, and to pass on: "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out!" and, "Who has known the mind of the Lord?" "And who has reached the farthest bounds of his wisdom?" says Job. Who is wise and will understand these things, and will not measure what is beyond measurement by what is beyond reach? Projections and recesses, great things and small, the rises and dips of the earth—from these beauty is composed and [?] through their relation to one another. For with a craftsman too, the disorder and unevenness of the material for the time being is very artful, if he has prepared it for the construction of some work; and we too grasp and acknowledge it when we behold the finished beauty of what he has made. But he is neither unskilled, as we are, nor are these things governed without order, simply because their reason is not known to us.

32. But if we must also offer some image of our condition, we are not far from those who are seasick and dizzy, who think that everything is spinning when they themselves are spinning. So it is with these people of whom we are speaking. For they will not allow God to be wiser than themselves when they grow dizzy at any of the things that happen.

…since we ought to labour over the reasoning, for perhaps the truth will be granted to diligence; or else to think these things through together with those wiser and more spiritual than ourselves, since this too is a gift, and not given to all; or to hunt for the truth by purity of life, and to seek wisdom from Wisdom himself. But others (oh, the ignorance!) turn to the easier course and falsely accuse the universe of irrationality, when it is they who do not know its reason. They are wise through ignorance, or rather, if I may put it so, unwise and senseless through excess of wisdom. This is why some have made chance and spontaneity their doctrine: notions truly spontaneous and made up at random. Others have made it the power of the stars, which weave our affairs irrationally and inescapably, as they please, or rather are themselves compelled to weave them; and the conjunctions and retreats of certain planets and fixed stars, and a motion that rules the universe. Still others, each bringing to the wretched human race whatever he had imagined, have introduced it, dividing up into various opinions and names whatever part of Providence was beyond their reach and beyond their sight. And there are some who have even accused Providence of great poverty. They suppose that the things above us are governed by it, but shrink from bringing it down as far as us, who need it most, as though afraid that by having more people benefit they would show the benefactor to be better, or that God would grow weary of doing good to more people. 31. But let these, as I said, be cast aside, since the Word has well anticipated and repelled them: "For their senseless heart became futile," it says; "claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God," insulting with myths and shadows the Providence that runs through all things. As for us, let us not tell such marvels ourselves, if we have any care for reason, being rational beings and servants of the Word; nor let us accept those who hold such opinions, even if their tongues run smoothly in absurd arguments and doctrines and they charm us with novelty. Rather, let us believe that God is the maker and fashioner of all things (for how could the universe have come to exist unless someone gave it being and fitted it together?), and let us also acknowledge Providence, which holds this universe together and binds it; since a provider too [?]… (81) For "senseless" the Regii a, c, d and the Jesuit manuscript read "uneducated." Others read "they wish."

…others less so, as though it were not about something great or very urgent. Rather, all of them, and each with earnestness, enjoin this either first or among the first things, sometimes exhorting, sometimes threatening, sometimes reproaching, and at times also praising those who do right, so that by constant reminder they may make the commandment effective. "Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise," says the Lord. Who does not fear the Lord when he arises? And: "Arise, O Lord my God, let your hand be lifted up; do not forget the poor." Let us pray to be spared such a lifting up, and let us not wish to see his hand raised against the disobedient, still less brought down upon the hard-hearted. And: "He did not forget the cry of the poor"; and: "The poor will not be forgotten forever"; and: "His eyes look upon the poor" (the eye being better and more sovereign than the eyelid), "but his eyelids examine the children of men": the lesser and secondary oversight, as one might call it. 36. Perhaps someone will say: "These things are said about the poor and needy who are wronged." I do not dispute it; but let this too spur you on to love of others. For if there is so much concern for them when they are wronged, clearly the favour is all the greater when they are treated well. For if he who dishonours the poor man provokes the one who made him, he who cares for the creature honours the Creator. Again, when you hear, "The poor and the rich met one another, but the Lord made them both," do not suppose that he made the one poor and the other rich, so that you may rise up all the more against the poor. For it is not clear that such a division comes from God. Rather, both alike, it says, are God's handiwork, even if their outward circumstances are unequal. Let this shame you into sympathy and brotherly love, so that when you are puffed up by those outward things, you may be humbled by this, and become more modest than you were. What else? "He who has mercy on the poor lends to God," it says. Who would not accept such a debtor, who will repay the loan in due time with interest? And again: "By almsgiving and faithfulness sins are purged away." (7) "O my God": [?] lacking in [?]. (9) "The harder-hearted": Regii a, b, c and [?] read "the hard-hearted." (10) Others read "will be forgotten" [variant spelling]. (12) "And secondary": "and" is lacking in Colbert 1. Patrologia Graeca XXXV.

37. Let us then be cleansed by showing mercy; let us wash away with this good cleansing herb the filth and stains of our souls, and be made white, some as wool, others as snow, in proportion to our compassion. Let me say something still more fearful. Suppose you have no fracture, no bruise, no inflamed wound, no leprosy of the soul, no spot or shining mark, which the law cleansed only a little and which need Christ to heal them. Even so, at least revere him who was wounded and weakened for our sake; and you will show him reverence if you show yourself kind and humane to a member of Christ. But suppose the robber and tyrant of our souls has perhaps wounded you badly, having caught you unarmed and unprepared, whether going down from Jerusalem to Jericho or somewhere else, so that you might fittingly say, "My wounds have grown foul and festered because of my folly." If you are in such a state that you do not even seek the cure, nor know the way to your healing, then alas for the wound indeed, and for the depth of your misery! But if you have not yet entirely despaired, and are not incurable, go to the Physician and entreat him. Heal wounds by wounds, gain like by like; or rather, be healed of greater ills by lesser gifts. He will say to your soul, "I am your salvation"; and, "Your faith has saved you"; and, "See, you have been made well"; and all the words of loving-kindness, if only he sees you showing loving-kindness to those who suffer. 38. "Blessed," it says, "are the merciful, for they will receive mercy." Mercy does not stand last among the beatitudes. And: "Blessed is he who considers the poor and needy"; and: "Good is the man who shows pity and lends"; and: "All day long the righteous man shows mercy and lends." Let us seize the blessing; let us be called considerate; let us become good. Do not let even the night interrupt your mercy. Do not say, "Go away and come back, and tomorrow I will give to you." Let nothing come between the impulse and the good deed. This alone admits no delay: loving-kindness. "Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house," and do this with eagerness. "He who shows mercy," it says, "with cheerfulness"; and your good deed is doubled by your readiness. For what is done out of grief or under compulsion is graceless and without beauty. We should celebrate our good deeds, not lament… (26) "Who will heal": one of the Regii and Nicetas read "who heals." (28) "You are" [subjunctive]: many read "you are" [indicative].

…kindness. "If you remove the bond," it says, "and the pointing of the finger," by which I mean pettiness and scrutiny, that is, hesitation, and the word of grumbling, what will happen? Something great and marvellous! What a reward this has, and how great! "Your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will spring up quickly." Who then does not long for light and [healing?]…

39. I revere also Christ's money-box, which calls us to feed the poor; and the agreement of Paul and Peter, who, when they divided the Gospel between them, made the poor their common concern; and the perfection of the young man, which was defined and laid down by law as giving what he had to the poor. Do you think love of others is not a necessity for you but a matter of choice? Not a law but advice? I too would very much like that, and once supposed it. But the left hand frightens me, and the goats, and the reproaches they receive from him who set them there. They were condemned to that place not because they had robbed, or committed sacrilege, or adultery, or done any other forbidden thing, but because they had not cared for Christ in those who were in need. 40. So if you will listen to me at all, servants of Christ, brothers and fellow heirs, while there is time let us visit Christ, care for Christ, feed Christ, clothe Christ, welcome Christ, honour Christ: not with a table only, as some did; nor with ointments, as Mary did; nor only with a tomb, as Joseph of Arimathea did; nor with burial spices, as Nicodemus did, who loved Christ by halves; nor with gold, frankincense and myrrh, as the Magi did before all these. Rather, since the Master of all desires mercy and not sacrifice, and compassion is worth more than tens of thousands of fat lambs, let us bring him this through those in need, and those who today lie cast upon the ground, so that when we depart from here they may receive us into the eternal dwellings, in Christ himself our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen. (38) "And marvellous": "and" is lacking in one of the Regii [?]. Then in a scholion "marvellous" [θαυμάσιον], explained [?] as "wonderful" [θαυμαστόν]. (40) "Made the poor partners", etc.: one of the Regii [?]. The Jesuit manuscript reads "made the poor a common work" [?]. Nicetas reads "[made] the care of the poor common." (41) "If then … at all": in most manuscripts, "if then" [εἰ δ' οὖν]. (42) "Let us care for Christ": these words are lacking in some [?]. (43) "Let us clothe Christ", for "let us clothe ourselves with [Christ]." [?] Regii a, c [?]. (46) "In Christ himself": one of the Regii reads "in the Christ himself" [with the article]. (47) "Glory": some add "and the power."
